These steps work if you use windows:

BACKUP

  1. ensure thunderbird is not running on PC
  2. enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key
  3. this should open windows file explorer in Appdata\roaming folder
  4. highlight the Thunderbird folder and copy to external media

RESTORE

  1. ensure thunderbird is installed, run once, and NOT running
  2. enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key
  3. delete the thunderbird folder
  4. you should be in Appdata\roaming folder , copy&paste the exported Thunderbird folder there.
  5. start thunderbird and all should be there

content:
Please note: a failed password does not necessarily mean the password is wrong. It could be the server settings are wrong or rejected for another reason.

Any mail account password can only be created/modified in the webmail account accessed via a browser for that email address.

Some servers insist that you use an 'app specific password' which you would also have to create whilst logged in webmail account, then it's used instead of regular password in third party email client such as Thunderbird.

Some servers insist that authentication uses Oauth2 such as Gmail and Yahoo.

Thunderbird will store passwords and use them to gain access to the server. They would be stored in this location:

  • Settings > Privacy & Security
  • Scroll down to Passwords section
  • click on 'Saved Passwords'
  • click on 'Show Passwords'

You can tell which account as username = full email address You will find there are two line - incoming and smtp for each account unless account uses OAuth. If you only use Oauth and you have updated your webmail account password, you may need to reset. That means deleting the line that has the Oauth password and go through authentication to get a new Oauth password. Otherwise: After modifying any password in your webmail account this is where you can update the stored password.

  • Right click on each line and select 'Edit Password'
  • completely clear all contents and carefully type in the updated/new password.
  • Click on 'Close'

After updating any password exit Thunderbird, allow a few moments then restart Thunderbird.

The above is generic advise. To offer best advise it would be helpful to provide a lot more information when asking a question.

What OS do you use ? Windows 11, MAC or Linux etc ? What version of Thunderbird are you using? Where did you get the Thunderbird download from ? Official Thunderbird webpage or via Windows App Store or Snap or Flatpak etc ?

What are the current server settings?

In Thunderbird

  • Help > Troubleshooting Information
  • scroll down to 'Mail and News accounts' section
  • Copy all the data and paste into this forum question - alternatively upload images of Account Settings > Server Settings and your SMTP server settings. - Do not just type them as you might make a typo error causing confusion.

Did you get any error message ? It would be helpful to upload an image file that shows the error message you are receiving.

content:
This isn't what Thunderbird is really made for, but you can finagle a way to do it...

- Install Thunderbird.

- On running it for the first time you will be prompted to set up a new account. There's no way to get around this.

- Set up a dummy account. The "Full Name" can be anything. Email address can be anything with the proper form - I used "test@invalid.com".

- At this point, the "Manual Configuration" option becomes available. Click it.

- The next page, "Incoming server settings" will have an option, "ADVANCED CONFIG". Click it and you will be presented with a dialog box saying, "This dialog will be closed and an account with the current settings will be created, even if the configuration is incorrect. Do you want to proceed?" Click OK.

- You will now have the non-active dummy account listed in <Account Settings>, plus the Local Folders pseudo account.

- Select the dummy account and click the red "Delete" button. You will be presented with a confirmation dialog box. Be sure to tick the "Remove message data" option.

You will now be left with only Local Folders, into which you can import your old email archive. Assuming your archive is left over from another Thunderbird installation, you can use Thunderbird's Import Tool to bring them into your Local Folders.

It may seem like a lot of initial work, but it's one-and-done. For me, the advantage would be familiarity with the interface and being able to use Thunderbird's search tools and add-ons. I have one such setup for a defunct AOL address that I keep for legal purposes but rarely if ever actually look at.
